claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state.
High-temperature and corrosive service exposure transforms the metastable solid solution through a diffusion-limited pathway.
During aging, Mg segregates from the original solid solution.
Mg segregation nucleates Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates grow and coalesce during continued exposure.
A critical Mg-rich intermetallic volume fraction exists beyond which protective properties decline.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates above the critical volume fraction disrupt the formation or persistence of a continuous protective oxide film.
Disruption of the protective oxide film reduces aqueous corrosion resistance.
Disruption of the protective oxide film reduces high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Service-condition aging will increase the volume fraction of Mg-rich precipitates relative to the initial metastable state.
Aged specimens will have poorer oxide-scale integrity and continuity than the initial metastable specimens.
Aged specimens will exhibit greater oxidation mass gain than the metastable baseline.
Aged specimens will exhibit higher corrosion current density or lower polarization resistance than the metastable baseline.
The as-processed metastable solid-solution state initially has superior corrosion and oxidation resistance.
The proposed pathway is relevant to prolonged oxidation in air around 900°C and corrosion exposure in 3.5 wt% NaCl.
